newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German M3 growth overshoots 1996 target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German M3 growth overshoots 1996 target.

text.p: The Bundesbank said on Thursday that growth in German M3 money supply slowed marginally in December, but admitted that its main monetary policy indicator had grown far beyond target in 1996.
The central bank said M3 grew at an annualised rate of 7.9 percent in December compared with its average level in the final quarter of 1995.

It grew by 8.1 percent in the final quarter of 1996 from the final quarter a year earlier. The Bundesbank had set a four to seven expansion corridor for money supply growth between the fourth quarter of 1995 and final quarter of 1996.
"In the entire fourth quarter of 1996 (M3 money supply) was 8.1 percent higher than in the fourth quarter 1995," the Bundesbank said.
"The money supply target for 1996, which looked for an expansion of M3 by four to seven percent in this period, was therefore overstepped," it added.
News that the central bank had overshot its target came as no surprise to financial markets, after double-digit growth rates earlier this year failed to slow as quickly as the Bundesbank had hoped.

The central bank, which blames uncertainty in bond markets throughout much of the year as a major factor in buoying M3 growth, acknowledged several months ago that its 1996 target had slipped out of reach.

But German debt prices slipped on the back of the firmer than expected December M3 figure, which dashed some hopes that the Bundesbank may nudge its main money market rate, the securities repurchase rate or repo, lower at its meeting today.

Most economists are expecting the Bundesbank to leave credit costs unchanged at the meeting, although there is a growing view that the central bank could lower the repo rate at a meeting later in the first or second quarter.
Economists said the main significance of the M3 data was that continued strong growth in M3 in the final month of 1996 meant that the base for next year's target would be high.
This meant that, due to statistical effects, M3 growth was likely to look weak in the early months of 1997. The Bundesbank has set a target of 3-1/2 to 6-1/2 percent growth for 1997.

Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London said in an initial reaction to the figures, "M3 growth was very strong in first half of last year so as a result the January figure will come in at a very low figure. The Bundesbank will use that an excuse to cut interest rates."

Michael Hochguertel at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt agreed, "I don't think the figure is very significant. The question is where M3 will be at the start of next year and I'd expect a rather low figure due to statistical effects." Hochguertel said the January growth figure was likely to be within or even below the 1997 growth target, adding that this could provide the basis for a small interest rate cut.
"There is a chance that the repo rate will come down a little," he said.

But Juergen Stanowsky, an economist at Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt, also believed that January M3 would be at the lower end of the corridor, but said he did not expect this to lead to an interest rate cut.

"I don't think rates will come down. The total value of the D-mark has come down. This will boost exports. So I would not paint a Doomsday picture. I don't think there are domestic reasons for the Bundesbank to cut rates," he said.
